query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled, trace amount of Zr to the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will cause Zr to segregate to the dual‐phase lamellar colony boundaries and form a nanoscale ductile interfacial phase. This modification is expected to strengthen boundary cohesion and facilitate dislocation transmission, which in turn will suppress microcrack initiation and propagation, leading to simultaneous improvements in room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a dual‐phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure that exhibits numerous internal boundaries serving as microcrack initiation sites, resulting in room-temperature brittleness despite high strength.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled trace addition of Zr during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under processing conditions (including thermal treatments) designed to promote Zr segregation to the internal lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The lamellar colony boundaries where Zr is expected to segregate and form a nanoscale ductile interfacial phase.
generation.mechanism: The added Zr segregates to the internal boundaries, reducing the local interfacial energy and stabilizing a ductile interfacial phase. This phase enhances dislocation transmission during tensile deformation and increases cohesion at the boundaries, thereby delaying microcrack nucleation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional unmodified lamellar alloy, the Zr-doped alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength along with improved ductility, as evidenced by reduced microcracking and enhanced plastic deformation at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows high strength but suffers from brittle failure initiated at numerous internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected within a narrowly optimized Zr concentration and under processing conditions that promote its segregation; deviations in dopant concentration or processing may not yield the desired ductile interfacial phase or might destabilize the microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentration of Zr, the detailed nature (e.g., thickness and morphology) of the ductile interfacial phase, and the quantitative magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements remain to be precisely determined through experimental study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one set with a controlled trace addition of Zr (in the optimal concentration window) and one undoped set as the baseline. Subject both to identical thermal treatments designed to promote dopant segregation. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and perform microscopic analyses (using TEM and EDS mapping) to assess the microstructure at the lamellar colony boundaries and monitor in situ crack initiation and propagation.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/EDS to verify Zr segregation and interfacial phase formation)
In situ observation of crack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Zr-doped samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the undoped baseline, or if microscopic analysis fails to confirm Zr segregation and the formation of a nanoscale ductile interfacial phase at the lamellar boundaries.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

chosen.why: This move directly inverts the conventional trade-off by targeting the interfacial regions—the sites of microcrack nucleation—thereby simultaneously increasing cohesion (boosting strength) and enhancing dislocation transmission (improving ductility). It builds on known evidence that targeted dopant segregation can reduce interfacial embrittlement and is implementable with standard alloy processing techniques.

frame.understanding: There is an incomplete understanding of how to reengineer colony boundaries to both suppress microcrack nucleation and promote favorable dislocation activity without compromising strength.
frame.method: A promising approach is to modify interfacial chemistry via a minor alloying addition (for example, adding trace amounts of boron) that segregates to the internal boundaries. The segregation could induce the formation of a nanoscale, ductile interfacial phase that both arrests crack propagation and facilitates effective dislocation transmission. The hypothesis predicts that the treated alloy will exhibit higher yield and ultimate strength as well as enhanced tensile ductility at room temperature compared to the original lamellar morphology, within a defined range of microalloying concentration and processing conditions. Prior evidence in similar alloy systems shows that boron additions can improve grain boundary cohesion and ductility, and an experiment—such as comparing tensile properties and in situ crack propagation in microalloyed versus unmodified samples—would falsify the hypothesis if no significant improvement or detrimental effects are observed.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (such as the study in PMC4145285) established a dual‐phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure by conventional casting and modest thermomechanical treatments, which achieved high strength but came at the cost of ductility. Subsequent studies across similar systems attempted various microstructural‐design and processing strategies – including thermomechanical refinement and minor compositional tweaks (e.g., adding Cr in refractory HEAs) – to improve performance. Although these approaches have increased yield and ultimate strengths, they have not prevented microcrack nucleation at the copious internal colony boundaries, leaving room-temperature tensile brittleness unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge remains how to redesign the internal boundaries of dual‐phase lamellar colonies so that they both arrest the nucleation and propagation of microcracks and simultaneously promote favorable dislocation motion, achieving a synergistic improvement in both tensile strength and ductility at room temperature.
decision.lever: interface dopant addition via controlled trace Zr (or Nb) incorporation
decision.why: Following the trend from conventional processing toward targeted interfacial modifications, the most plausible next step is to introduce a controlled dopant that segregates to the lamellar colony boundaries. This lever seeks to form a nanoscale ductile interfacial phase, which would reinforce boundary cohesion to arrest crack propagation while enhancing dislocation transmission during deformation. This strategy directly addresses the root-cause cues of microcrack initiation at dual-phase boundaries and occupies the niche where previous thermomechanical processing failed to balance strength and ductility.
